column2: Brawley is located in the Imperial Valley of southeastern California, supplied by the Colorado River via the All‑American Canal and local wells.
column3: The City of Brawley operates a potable water treatment plant to supply residents and agricultural users. The facility draws raw water from the Colorado River and treats it using conventional processes.
column4: The water treatment plant has a design capacity of 15 MGDhttps://www.brawley-ca.gov/departments/public-works/water-treatment-plant#:~:text=The%20City%20of%20Brawley%20Water
column5: Control%20Board%20Drinking%20Water%20Office. Population served is ~26 000. Production is typically below capacity but spikes during peak agricultural demand.
column6: Raw water is pumped, coagulated, flocculated, filtered and disinfected. Operators monitor flow, turbidity and chlorine residual. Distribution includes storage reservoirs and booster pumps.
column7: Drinking water must comply with California and U.S. EPA standards. The plant is permitted by the State Water Resources Control Board; disinfection processes ensure microbial safety.
column8: Seasonal demand peaks during summer; turbidity may increase during canal maintenance. Treatment plant performance remains stable with minor fluctuations in chemical dosing.
column9: The 2024 consumer confidence report lists pH ~7.9, sodium 110 mg/L, potassium 5.3 mg/L and vanadium 0.0039 mg/Lwww.brawley-ca.gov/assets/pwdocs/wtpdocs/2024_ccr.pdf#:~:text=2024%20330%20NA%20Runoff%2Fleaching%20from,NA%20Leaching%20from%20natural%20deposits. Other parameters are within regulatory limits; nitrate levels are generally low.
column10: Electricity is consumed for pumping and mixing; chemical use includes coagulants and chlorine. Energy use rises during peak irrigation season.
column11: Operators conduct daily monitoring for turbidity, chlorine, and pH; periodic laboratory analyses for metals, organics and coliform bacteria.
column12: Conventional coagulation/flocculation, gravity filtration and chlorination; potential upgrades may include advanced filtration or UV disinfection.
column13: Dependence on Colorado River water; vulnerability to drought; high dissolved solids and salinity from agricultural return flows.
column14: Water conservation, desalination of agricultural drainage, and potential adoption of advanced filtration to remove emerging contaminants.

column2: The Imperial Valley’s waterways, including the New River and Alamo River, discharge to the Salton Sea. Urban runoff and agricultural drainage may carry plastics.
column3: No published studies have quantified microplastics in Brawley’s drinking water or wastewater. Regional studies suggest microplastics are present in surface waters of Southern California.
column4: Without site‑specific data, microplastic loads are unknown. Comparative studies in urban rivers show concentrations of 0.05–16 particles/m³ftp.sccwrp.org/pub/download/DOCUMENTS/TechnicalReports/1389_MPLosAngelesSanGabrielRivers.pdf#:~:text=contaminants%20in%20the%20watershed%20may,in%20the%20San, while stormwater in nearby Tijuana had 66–191 particles/Lhttps://www.frontiersin.org/journals/environmental-science/articles/10.3389/fenvs.2023.1090267/full#:~:text=%28Sutton%20et%20al.%2C%202019%29,in%20stormwater%20microplastic%20concentrations%20amongst; these values indicate potential ranges but cannot be applied directly.
column5: Water treatment relies on conventional filtration, which can remove some microplastics. There is no dedicated microplastic monitoring or removal technology at the Brawley plant.
column6: California’s microplastics monitoring requirements will eventually apply to small systems like Brawley, but compliance timelines are still being developed.
column8: Co‑occurring parameters such as total suspended solids and turbidity are monitored; high salinity may influence particle behavior.
column9: Additional microplastic removal would increase energy use if advanced filtration were installed.
column10: Standard methods for microplastics include filtration, digestion and spectroscopic analysis; these have not yet been implemented locally.
column11: Potential upgrades could include granular media filters, membrane filtration or advanced oxidation for microplastic and organic contaminant removal.
column12: Lack of baseline data, possible microplastic inputs from agricultural plastic mulch and litter, and limited funding for advanced monitoring.
column13: Regional research partnerships could assess microplastic levels and inform mitigation strategies; public education on plastic use reduction.

column2: The Imperial Valley is an agricultural region; runoff from farms and animal operations enters canals that supply Brawley’s water.
column3: Potential contaminants include nitrates, pesticides, salts, selenium and pathogens. Industrial discharges are minimal, but agricultural return flows carry significant loads.
column4: Brawley’s 2024 report provides limited quantitative data; pH 7.9, sodium 110 mg/L, potassium 5.3 mg/L and vanadium 0.0039 mg/Lwww.brawley-ca.gov/assets/pwdocs/wtpdocs/2024_ccr.pdf#:~:text=2024%20330%20NA%20Runoff%2Fleaching%20from,NA%20Leaching%20from%20natural%20deposits. Historical data indicate total dissolved solids often exceed 1 000 mg/L and hardness >300 mg/L due to Colorado River water.
column5: Treatment reduces turbidity and microbes but cannot remove dissolved salts or some pesticides. The city participates in regional programs to reduce agricultural runoff.
column6: Water quality must meet primary MCLs; high TDS and hardness are aesthetic issues addressed by secondary standards. Agricultural dischargers are regulated under the Colorado River Basin Water Board’s Irrigated Lands Program.
column7: TDS and hardness vary seasonally with irrigation return flows; nitrate concentrations may increase after fertilizer application but rarely exceed the MCL.
column8: Parameters of interest include TDS, hardness, nitrate, arsenic and pesticide residues. Brawley’s report lists vanadium at 0.0039 mg/L, reflecting trace metals levelswww.brawley-ca.gov/assets/pwdocs/wtpdocs/2024_ccr.pdf#:~:text=2024%20330%20NA%20Runoff%2Fleaching%20from,NA%20Leaching%20from%20natural%20deposits.
column9: Removal of salts would require energy‑intensive processes such as reverse osmosis, which are not used; current operations have moderate energy demand.
column10: Routine sampling for regulated contaminants; participation in regional groundwater quality monitoring. Some pesticides may not be routinely tested.
column11: Potential improvements include blending with lower‑salinity sources, ion exchange or desalination, and best management practices in agriculture to reduce nutrient runoff.
column12: High salinity and hardness, pesticide contamination from agriculture, and limited funding for advanced treatment.
column13: Agricultural conservation programs and constructed wetlands could reduce pollutant loads; adoption of desalination or concentrate management for drinking water supply.

column2: Municipal supply to Brawley and surrounding communities is drawn from the All‑American Canal and wells; distribution lines serve residential and agricultural customers.
column3: Water quality is characterized by high mineral content and meets primary standards but may exceed secondary aesthetic standards.
column4: pH ~7.9; sodium 110 mg/L; potassium 5.3 mg/L; vanadium 0.0039 mg/L as reported in 2024www.brawley-ca.gov/assets/pwdocs/wtpdocs/2024_ccr.pdf#:~:text=2024%20330%20NA%20Runoff%2Fleaching%20from,NA%20Leaching%20from%20natural%20deposits. TDS often ~1 000 mg/L, hardness >300 mg/L (not explicitly stated in the report).
column5: Treatment plant operators control coagulation and disinfection to remove particulates and pathogens; no processes for salinity removal.
column6: Water meets primary MCLs for nitrate, arsenic, lead and copper. Secondary standards for taste and odor may be exceeded due to TDS and hardness.
column7: Mineral concentrations vary with Colorado River water quality and seasonal agricultural return flows.
column8: Typical indicators include turbidity (<0.3 NTU), TDS (~1 000 mg/L), hardness (~300 mg/L as CaCO₃), nitrate (well below 10 mg/L).
column9: Energy use linked to pumping and chemical dosing.
column10: Routine monitoring for regulated contaminants; periodic testing for trace metals and unregulated substances.
column11: Conventional treatment only; potential addition of desalination or ion exchange would improve quality.
column12: High salinity limits reuse and may affect crops; drought and climate change may reduce Colorado River deliveries.
column13: Water conservation, reuse of treated wastewater for agriculture, and regional desalination projects.
